lessons.title: The second wave: more roots, prefixes and suffixes
lessons.body:
## Doubling your vocabulary

The first pass gave you roughly a hundred parts. This lesson adds about fifty more, chosen because they appear in charts and orders you will read in your first month. Decode them the same way: suffix, prefix, root.

## More roots

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `aden/o` | gland | `adenopathy`, gland disease |
| `adip/o`, `lip/o` | fat | `lipoma`, a fatty tumor |
| `chondr/o` | cartilage | `costochondritis` |
| `cost/o` | rib | `intercostal` |
| `erythr/o` | red | `erythrocyte`, red blood cell |
| `leuk/o` | white | `leukocyte`, white blood cell |
| `melan/o` | black | `melanoma` |
| `cyan/o` | blue | `cyanosis` |
| `gloss/o`, `lingu/o` | tongue | `sublingual` |
| `hydr/o` | water | `hydrocephalus` |
| `mamm/o`, `mast/o` | breast | `mastectomy` |
| `nas/o` | nose | `nasogastric` |
| `necr/o` | death of tissue | `necrosis` |
| `onych/o` | nail | `onychomycosis` |
| `phren/o` | diaphragm, or mind | `phrenic nerve` |
| `pleur/o` | lining of the lung | `pleuritis` |
| `pyel/o` | renal pelvis | `pyelonephritis` |
| `salping/o` | tube | `salpingectomy` |
| `spir/o` | breathing | `spirometry` |
| `splen/o` | spleen | `splenomegaly` |
| `spondyl/o` | vertebra | `spondylosis` |
| `ten/o`, `tendin/o` | tendon | `tendinitis` |
| `thyr/o` | thyroid gland | `hyperthyroidism` |
| `xer/o` | dry | `xerostomia`, dry mouth |

## More prefixes

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `ab-` | away from | `abduction` |
| `ad-` | toward | `adduction` |
| `dia-` | through, complete | `diaphoresis` |
| `ecto-`, `exo-` | outside, out | `ectopic pregnancy` |
| `iso-` | equal, same | `isotonic` |
| `macro-` | large | `macrocytic` |
| `micro-` | small | `microcytic` |
| `mal-` | bad, poor | `malaise`, `malabsorption` |
| `neo-` | new | `neoplasm` |
| `pan-` | all | `pancytopenia` |
| `per-` | through | `percutaneous` |
| `syn-`, `sym-` | together | `syndrome`, `symphysis` |
| `auto-` | self | `autoimmune` |
| `nulli-`, `primi-`, `multi-` | none, first, many | `nulliparous`, `primigravida` |

## More suffixes

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `-cyte` | cell | `leukocyte` |
| `-desis` | surgical fusion | `arthrodesis` |
| `-ectasis` | dilation, expansion | `atelectasis` |
| `-lysis` | breakdown, separation | `hemolysis` |
| `-malacia` | softening | `osteomalacia` |
| `-penia` | deficiency | `thrombocytopenia` |
| `-phasia` | speech | `aphasia` |
| `-plasia` | formation, growth | `hyperplasia` |
| `-ptosis` | drooping, falling | `blepharoptosis` |
| `-rrhaphy` | surgical suturing | `herniorrhaphy` |
| `-stasis` | stopping, controlling | `hemostasis` |
| `-stenosis` | narrowing | `aortic stenosis` |
| `-tripsy` | crushing | `lithotripsy` |
| `-trophy` | development, nourishment | `hypertrophy`, `atrophy` |

> **Key:** `-penia` is deficiency and `-osis` is an abnormal condition, usually an excess. `Leukopenia` is too few white cells; `leukocytosis` is too many. One suffix flips the entire meaning.

## How to drill them

Memorizing a list front to back does not survive a shift. Three drills work better.

1. **Build, do not recall.** Given a meaning, assemble the word. Inflammation of a tendon becomes `tendinitis`. Too few platelets becomes `thrombocytopenia`. Surgical fusion of a joint becomes `arthrodesis`.
2. **Decode cold.** Take any unfamiliar word off a chart and break it apart before you look it up. `Nephrosclerosis` is hardening of the kidney. `Pancytopenia` is a deficiency of all blood cell lines.
3. **Drill the near-twins together**, because that is where errors live.

| Pair | Difference |
|---|---|
| `-penia` / `-osis` | too few / too many |
| `hyper-` / `hypo-` | above / below normal |
| `arteri/o` / `arthr/o` | artery / joint |
| `ileum` / `ilium` | small bowel segment / hip bone |
| `mucus` / `mucous` | the substance / the adjective |
| `-ectasis` / `-stenosis` | widened / narrowed |

> **Trap:** `Ileum` and `ilium` are pronounced identically and sit inches apart in the body. An ileostomy opens the small bowel; the iliac crest is a bone. Spell them deliberately.

> **On shift:** When you meet a word you cannot decode, it is usually an eponym, a drug name or an acronym, and none of those are built from parts. Recognizing that instantly saves you from trying to decode something that has no parts to find.
keyPoints: Color roots carry meaning: erythr/o red, leuk/o white, melan/o black, cyan/o blue.
-penia is deficiency and -osis is an abnormal condition or excess, so leukopenia and leukocytosis are opposites.
-stenosis is narrowing and -ectasis is dilation; -rrhaphy is suturing and -desis is surgical fusion.
Drill by building words from meanings and decoding unfamiliar words cold, not by reciting lists.
A word you cannot decode is usually an eponym, a drug name, or an acronym, none of which have parts.

checks.q: A patient's chart reads thrombocytopenia. What does that mean?
choices: Too many platelets
A clot in a vein
Too few platelets
Destruction of red blood cells
checks.why: Thromb/o is clot, cyt/o is cell, and -penia is deficiency, so it is a deficiency of clotting cells, meaning platelets. Too many would be thrombocytosis, and destruction of red cells is hemolysis.

checks.q: Which pair means narrowing and widening respectively?
choices: -stenosis and -ectasis
-penia and -osis
-malacia and -sclerosis
-plasia and -trophy
checks.why: -stenosis is narrowing, as in aortic stenosis, and -ectasis is dilation or expansion, as in bronchiectasis. -penia and -osis are deficiency and excess, and -malacia and -sclerosis are softening and hardening.

checks.q: Decode pancytopenia.
choices: Inflammation of the whole pancreas
A deficiency of all blood cell lines
An excess of all blood cell lines
Surgical removal of the pancreas
checks.why: Pan- is all, cyt/o is cell, and -penia is deficiency, so all cell lines are low. The pancreas root is pancreat/o, not pan-, which is a common misread.

lessons.title: Reading a lab report and an imaging report
lessons.body:
## What a lab report is telling you

Every result has three parts: the value, the reference range, and a flag. A result is not abnormal because it is unusual; it is flagged because it sits outside the range that laboratory established for that population and that instrument.

A few framing words come up constantly.

- **Reference range** — the interval covering most healthy people, typically the middle `95%`
- **Critical value**, also called a panic value — so dangerous the lab phones it in rather than posting it
- **Hemolyzed** — red cells broke during collection or transport, which falsely raises potassium and voids the specimen
- **Pending** — collected, not resulted
- **Add-on** — a test ordered later on a specimen already in the lab

## The two panels you will see most

**Complete blood count (`CBC`).** White cells (`WBC`), red cells (`RBC`), hemoglobin (`Hgb`), hematocrit (`Hct`), and platelets (`Plt`). The differential splits the white cells into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. A rise in immature neutrophils, called **bands**, is a **left shift**, which suggests the marrow is releasing cells early to fight an infection.

**Basic metabolic panel (`BMP`).** Sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate (often labelled `CO2`), blood urea nitrogen (`BUN`), creatinine, glucose and calcium. The comprehensive panel (`CMP`) adds liver values: albumin, total protein, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, `AST` and `ALT`.

Notice how the names decode. Hyper- or hypo- plus the substance plus `-emia` gives you the abnormality: `hyperkalemia` is high potassium (`kal/i`), `hyponatremia` is low sodium (`natr/o`), `hypercalcemia` is high calcium.

| Common single tests | What it is asking |
|---|---|
| Troponin | Has heart muscle been damaged |
| `BNP` | Is the heart stretched, as in heart failure |
| `D-dimer` | Is there evidence of clot breakdown |
| Lactate | Is tissue running without enough oxygen |
| `INR`, `PT`, `PTT` | How fast is blood clotting |
| Urinalysis | Leukocyte esterase and nitrites suggest infection |
| Culture and sensitivity | Which organism, and which antibiotics kill it |

> **Key:** A blood gas reports `pH`, `PaCO2`, `PaO2` and `HCO3`. `PaCO2` is the lung's number and `HCO3` is the kidney's number, which is exactly the respiratory-versus-metabolic split you already know.

## What an imaging report is telling you

Radiology reports are written in a fixed order, and the order matters.

1. **Technique** — what was done: `CT` abdomen with intravenous contrast, portable chest radiograph, and so on
2. **Comparison** — what prior study this was measured against
3. **Findings** — everything the radiologist observed, including normal structures
4. **Impression** — the conclusion, numbered by importance

> **On shift:** Read the impression first. It is the radiologist's answer. The findings section is the evidence, and it lists normal anatomy too, which is why it looks alarming when read cold.

## The vocabulary inside the report

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `AP`, `PA`, lateral | The direction the beam passed: front to back, back to front, side |
| Portable | Taken at the bedside; usually `AP` and less sharp |
| Radiopaque | Blocks x-rays, appears white: bone, metal, contrast |
| Radiolucent | Passes x-rays, appears dark: air, fat |
| Opacity | An area whiter than it should be |
| Lucency | An area darker than it should be |
| Infiltrate, consolidation | Fluid or cells filling alveoli, as in pneumonia |
| Effusion | Fluid in a space, as in pleural effusion |
| Atelectasis | Collapsed or unexpanded lung |
| Free air | Air outside a hollow organ, suggesting perforation |
| Cardiomegaly | Enlarged cardiac silhouette |
| With contrast | Dye given to make vessels or organs stand out |

Two phrases carry more weight than they appear to. **No acute cardiopulmonary process** means nothing new and urgent was seen; it does not mean the chest is normal. **Clinical correlation recommended** means the picture alone cannot settle the question and the answer depends on the patient in front of you.

> **Trap:** An **incidental finding** is something real that was not what anybody was looking for, such as a nodule found on a trauma scan. It is not a reason to relax and it is not the diagnosis; it is a separate problem that needs its own follow-up.
keyPoints: Every lab value comes with a reference range and a flag; critical values are phoned rather than posted.
A hemolyzed specimen falsely raises potassium and must be redrawn.
A left shift means immature neutrophils (bands) are being released early, suggesting infection.
Hyper- or hypo- plus the substance plus -emia names the abnormality: hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia.
Read the imaging impression first; no acute cardiopulmonary process means nothing new and urgent, not normal.

checks.q: A potassium result is flagged critical at 6.8 mEq/L and the specimen is noted as hemolyzed. What does that mean?
choices: The result is confirmed and must be treated immediately without question
Red cells broke during collection and released potassium, so the value is unreliable and needs a redraw
Hemolysis falsely lowers potassium, so the true value is higher
Hemolysis affects only the hemoglobin measurement
checks.why: Potassium is overwhelmingly intracellular, so ruptured red cells spill it into the sample and falsely raise the reported value. A hemolyzed critical potassium is redrawn, though a genuinely sick patient is not ignored while that happens.

checks.q: Which section of a radiology report should you read first, and why?
choices: Technique, because it states the study performed
Findings, because it is the most detailed
Impression, because it is the radiologist's conclusion
Comparison, because it establishes the trend
checks.why: The impression is the answer, numbered by importance. The findings section lists normal structures alongside abnormal ones, which reads alarmingly out of context, and technique and comparison are supporting detail.

checks.q: A chest radiograph report concludes: no acute cardiopulmonary process. What does that permit you to conclude?
choices: The chest is entirely normal
The patient cannot have a pulmonary embolism
Nothing new and urgent was seen on this study
All chronic findings have resolved
checks.why: The phrase means no new emergency finding on this modality. Chronic abnormalities may still be present, and several serious diagnoses, including pulmonary embolism, routinely have a normal chest radiograph.

lessons.title: Reading a medication order: the sig line
lessons.body:
## What a sig is

The instruction line on a prescription is the **sig**, from the Latin `signa`, meaning write. It tells the patient what to take, how much, by which route, how often, and for how long.

A complete order has six parts, and a missing part is a query, not an assumption.

1. Drug name
2. Strength and dose form
3. Route
4. Frequency
5. Duration or quantity
6. Indication, meaning what it is for

## Frequency, the part people get wrong

| Abbreviation | From | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `BID` | bis in die | twice daily |
| `TID` | ter in die | three times daily |
| `QID` | quater in die | four times daily |
| `q4h`, `q6h`, `q8h` | quaque | every 4, 6 or 8 hours |
| `qhs` | hora somni | at bedtime |
| `ac` | ante cibum | before meals |
| `pc` | post cibum | after meals |
| `PRN` | pro re nata | as needed |
| `ATC` | | around the clock |
| `ad lib` | ad libitum | as the patient wishes |
| `STAT` | statim | immediately |

> **Key:** `QID` and `q6h` are not the same instruction. `QID` means four doses during waking hours; `q6h` means every six hours around the clock, which wakes the patient at night. For an antibiotic that difference changes blood levels.

## Form, route and quantity

Forms: `tab` tablet, `cap` capsule, `susp` suspension, `soln` solution, `elix` elixir, `supp` suppository, `ung` ointment, `cr` cream, `gtt` drops, `MDI` metered-dose inhaler, `neb` nebulizer solution, `patch` transdermal. The letters `ER`, `XR`, `SR`, `CR`, `LA` and `DR` all mean the tablet releases slowly and must not be crushed.

Routes: `PO` by mouth, `PR` rectally, `SL` sublingual, `IV` intravenous, `IVP` intravenous push, `IVPB` intravenous piggyback, `IM` intramuscular, `subQ` subcutaneous, `IN` intranasal, `IO` intraosseous, `ID` intradermal, `top` topical, `inh` inhaled, `NG` or `PEG` through a feeding tube.

Quantities: Roman numerals appear as `i`, `ii`, `iii` for one, two and three tablets, and `ss` means one half. `disp` is dispense, `qs` is a sufficient quantity, and `mEq` is milliequivalents, used for electrolytes like potassium.

**Intravenous fluids** have their own shorthand: `NS` is normal saline, `D5W` is `5%` dextrose in water, `LR` is lactated Ringer's, `KVO` or `TKO` means keep the line barely open. Drip rates are written in `gtts/min`, drops per minute, and the tubing's **drop factor** is printed on the package, commonly `10`, `15` or `60 gtts/mL`.

## Reading real lines

| Sig | What it says |
|---|---|
| `Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily` | Ten milligrams by mouth once a day |
| `Metformin 500 mg PO BID with meals` | Five hundred milligrams by mouth twice daily with food |
| `Atorvastatin 40 mg PO qhs` | Forty milligrams by mouth at bedtime |
| `Ondansetron 4 mg SL q8h PRN nausea, disp #20` | Four milligrams under the tongue every eight hours as needed for nausea, dispense twenty |
| `Albuterol 2 puffs MDI q4h PRN SOB` | Two puffs from the inhaler every four hours as needed for shortness of breath |
| `Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN pain, max 3 g/24h` | Six hundred fifty milligrams by mouth every six hours as needed, never exceeding three grams a day |
| `Amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID x 10 days` | Three times daily for ten days, which is thirty capsules |

> **Trap:** `HS` is on most institutional avoid lists because it means both at bedtime and half strength. Write at bedtime. Similarly, `gtt` in an eye order means a drop, while `gtt` on a fluid order means a drip rate; the context is the only thing separating them.

> **On shift:** When an order is missing a route, a frequency, or an indication, you do not fill in the gap from memory. You ask. The most common serious errors are not misread words; they are assumed ones.
keyPoints: A complete order names the drug, strength and form, route, frequency, duration or quantity, and the indication.
QID means four waking doses while q6h means every six hours around the clock, including overnight.
qhs is at bedtime, ac is before meals, pc is after meals, PRN is as needed, STAT is immediately.
ER, XR, SR, CR, LA and DR mark extended-release tablets that must not be crushed.
HS is ambiguous between at bedtime and half strength, so write the words out; a missing element is a query, never an assumption.

checks.q: An order reads: Amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID x 7 days. How many capsules will be dispensed?
checks.why: TID is three times daily, so three capsules a day for seven days is twenty-one. Fourteen would be BID and twenty-eight would be QID.

checks.q: What is the practical difference between QID and q6h for an antibiotic?
choices: There is none; both mean four doses a day
QID is four waking doses; q6h is every six hours around the clock including overnight
q6h means four doses only if the patient is awake
QID means every six hours and q6h means as needed
checks.why: Both total four doses in a day, but q6h spaces them evenly and wakes the patient, which keeps drug levels steadier. QID clusters them into waking hours, leaving a long overnight gap.

checks.q: Why is HS discouraged on medication orders?
choices: It is Latin and no longer taught
It can mean at bedtime or half strength
It is easily confused with IV
It applies only to inhaled medications
checks.why: HS carries two incompatible meanings, at bedtime and half strength, so the safe form is to write the words. It is on most institutional avoid lists for that reason.

lessons.title: Naming an operation from its parts
lessons.body:
## The suffix tells you what was done to the organ

Surgical names are unusually honest. The root names the target and the suffix names the action, so you can reconstruct the operation without having seen it.

| Suffix | Action | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `-ectomy` | remove it | `appendectomy` |
| `-otomy` | cut into it | `thoracotomy` |
| `-ostomy` | create a lasting opening | `colostomy` |
| `-plasty` | repair or reshape it | `angioplasty` |
| `-pexy` | fix it in place | `orchiopexy` |
| `-rrhaphy` | sew it | `herniorrhaphy` |
| `-desis` | fuse it so it stops moving | `arthrodesis`, `pleurodesis` |
| `-centesis` | puncture it to withdraw fluid | `paracentesis` |
| `-tripsy` | crush it | `lithotripsy` |
| `-scopy` | look inside it | `arthroscopy` |
| `-tome` | the instrument that cuts | `dermatome` |

## The three that get confused, settled

The airway set makes the distinction concrete.

- **Tracheotomy** — the trachea is cut into. A temporary act.
- **Tracheostomy** — a lasting opening is created and kept open. The stoma is the point.
- **Tracheectomy** — the trachea itself is removed. Rare, and a very different conversation.

The chest set is the one you will hear on shift.

- **Thoracentesis** — a needle drains fluid from the pleural space
- **Thoracostomy** — a chest tube is placed through the wall and stays
- **Thoracotomy** — the chest is opened surgically

> **Key:** `-otomy` is an act, `-ostomy` is an opening that persists, `-ectomy` is a removal. Three letters of difference, three different operations.

## How the surgery was reached

A second word names the approach rather than the action.

- **Open** — a full incision
- **Laparoscopic** — through small ports with a camera, abbreviated `lap`
- **Thoracoscopic** — the same idea in the chest
- **Percutaneous** — through the skin with a needle or catheter, no incision
- **Endoscopic** — through a natural opening
- **Exploratory laparotomy**, `ex-lap` — the abdomen is opened to find out what is wrong

So a `lap chole` is a laparoscopic cholecystectomy: the gallbladder removed through small ports.

## Operations you will hear named

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ORIF` | Open reduction internal fixation: a fracture is realigned and held with hardware |
| `CABG` | Coronary artery bypass graft, spoken as cabbage |
| `PCI` | Percutaneous coronary intervention, a catheter opening a coronary artery |
| `THA`, `TKA` | Total hip or knee arthroplasty, a joint replaced |
| Craniotomy | The skull is opened and the bone flap replaced |
| Craniectomy | The bone flap is left off to allow swelling |
| `PEG` | Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy, a feeding tube into the stomach |
| Colostomy, ileostomy | A lasting opening of colon or ileum onto the abdominal wall |
| `TURP` | Transurethral resection of the prostate |
| Fasciotomy | The fascia is cut to relieve compartment pressure |
| Escharotomy | Burned, rigid skin is cut to relieve constriction |
| Cricothyrotomy | An emergency airway through the cricothyroid membrane |
| Hysterectomy, oophorectomy, salpingectomy | Uterus, ovary, tube removed |
| `AKA`, `BKA` | Above-knee or below-knee amputation |

> **Trap:** Craniotomy and craniectomy differ by one syllable and by whether the patient still has a piece of skull. A craniectomy patient must not have pressure applied to that side of the head and often wears a protective helmet.

## Around the operation

`Pre-op`, `intra-op` and `post-op` mark before, during and after. `POD 2` is postoperative day two. `NPO` after midnight prevents aspiration under anesthesia. The **time-out** is the mandatory pause before incision in which the whole team confirms patient, procedure and site out loud.

> **On shift:** When a patient says they had their gallbladder out, ask whether it was laparoscopic or open. Four small scars and one long one imply very different recoveries, different pain expectations, and different complications.
keyPoints: The root names the target and the suffix names the action, so operations decode like any other built word.
-otomy is cutting into, -ostomy is a lasting opening, -ectomy is removal; tracheotomy, tracheostomy and tracheectomy are three different things.
Thoracentesis drains with a needle, thoracostomy places a chest tube, thoracotomy opens the chest surgically.
Approach words name how it was reached: open, laparoscopic, thoracoscopic, percutaneous, endoscopic.
Craniotomy replaces the bone flap and craniectomy leaves it off, which changes how the patient's head is handled.

checks.q: A patient has a chest tube placed for a pneumothorax. What is that procedure called?
choices: Thoracotomy
Thoracentesis
Thoracostomy
Thoracoplasty
checks.why: A tube placed through the chest wall that stays in place is a lasting opening, so -ostomy. Thoracotomy is surgical opening of the chest, thoracentesis is a needle drainage of fluid, and thoracoplasty is a reshaping procedure.

checks.q: What is the practical difference between a craniotomy and a craniectomy?
choices: A craniotomy uses a camera and a craniectomy does not
A craniotomy replaces the bone flap; a craniectomy leaves it off to allow for swelling
A craniectomy is done only on children
There is no difference; they are synonyms
checks.why: -otomy means cut into, with the bone replaced at the end, while -ectomy means removal, so the flap stays off. That patient's skull is unprotected on that side and must not have pressure applied.

checks.q: A note records lap chole, POD 1. What happened and when?
choices: A laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and this is the first day after surgery
An open colectomy performed one day ago
A laparotomy planned for postoperative day one
A laparoscopic colostomy with the patient still in the operating room
checks.why: Lap is laparoscopic, chole is the gallbladder, and the implied -ectomy makes it a gallbladder removal through small ports. POD 1 is postoperative day one.

lessons.title: Eponyms you will hear in the emergency department
lessons.body:
## Words with no parts

An **eponym** is a term named after a person or place. You cannot decode `Murphy's sign` the way you decode `pericarditis`, because there are no parts inside it. These must simply be learned, and the fastest way is to learn the maneuver, not the name.

> **Key:** For each eponym, hold three things: what you do or see, what it suggests, and how much you should trust it. The third item is the one most lists leave out.

## Abdominal

| Eponym | What you do or see | Suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Murphy's sign | Press under the right costal margin while the patient inhales; they stop the breath from pain | Acute cholecystitis |
| McBurney's point | Tenderness one third of the way from the right hip bone to the umbilicus | Appendicitis |
| Rovsing's sign | Pressing the left lower quadrant produces right lower quadrant pain | Appendicitis |
| Kehr's sign | Left shoulder pain, worse lying flat | Blood irritating the diaphragm, classically a ruptured spleen |
| Cullen's sign | Bruising around the umbilicus | Bleeding into the abdomen or retroperitoneum |
| Grey Turner's sign | Bruising in the flanks | Retroperitoneal bleeding, as in severe pancreatitis |

Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs take `24`–`48` hours to appear, so their absence early tells you nothing.

## Head, neck and neurologic

| Eponym | What you see | Suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Battle's sign | Bruising over the mastoid, behind the ear | Basilar skull fracture |
| Raccoon eyes | Bruising around both orbits with no direct eye trauma | Basilar skull fracture |
| Cushing's triad | Rising blood pressure, falling heart rate, irregular breathing | Rising intracranial pressure |
| Brudzinski's sign | Flexing the neck makes the hips and knees flex | Meningeal irritation |
| Kernig's sign | With the hip flexed, straightening the knee causes pain | Meningeal irritation |
| Babinski sign | Stroking the sole makes the big toe go up | Upper motor neuron lesion; normal under about age `2` |

## Chest and circulation

| Eponym | What you find | Suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Beck's triad | Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds | Cardiac tamponade |
| Levine's sign | The patient describes chest pain with a clenched fist over the sternum | Ischemic cardiac pain |
| Kussmaul's sign | Neck veins rise on inspiration instead of falling | Tamponade or constrictive pericarditis |
| Homans' sign | Calf pain when the foot is dorsiflexed | Historically deep vein thrombosis |
| Osborn or `J` wave | A hump at the end of the QRS on the ECG | Hypothermia |

> **Trap:** Homans' sign is the classic example of an eponym that survived its own evidence. It is neither sensitive nor specific for deep vein thrombosis, so a negative Homans' rules nothing out and a positive one proves nothing. Know the name; do not make decisions on it.

## Electrolytes and breathing

| Eponym | What you do or see | Suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Chvostek's sign | Tap the facial nerve in front of the ear; the face twitches | Low calcium |
| Trousseau's sign | Inflate a blood pressure cuff for `3` minutes; the hand goes into spasm | Low calcium, and the more reliable of the two |
| Kussmaul respirations | Deep, fast, sighing breaths | Metabolic acidosis, classically diabetic ketoacidosis |
| Cheyne-Stokes respirations | Cycles of deepening then shallowing breaths with pauses | Severe brain injury, end-stage illness |

Note that Kussmaul has two separate findings named after him, a breathing pattern and a neck vein sign. They are unrelated, and mixing them up is a common exam error.

> **On the exam:** Eponyms are exam favorites precisely because they cannot be reasoned out. Expect Beck's triad for tamponade, Cushing's triad for intracranial pressure, Battle's sign for basilar skull fracture, and Kehr's sign for splenic injury to appear almost verbatim.
keyPoints: Eponyms have no decodable parts; learn the maneuver, the meaning and the reliability.
Murphy's sign points to cholecystitis, McBurney's and Rovsing's to appendicitis, Kehr's to splenic injury.
Battle's sign and raccoon eyes both suggest basilar skull fracture; Cushing's triad means rising intracranial pressure.
Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) means cardiac tamponade.
Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs indicate low calcium; Homans' sign is unreliable and should not drive decisions.

checks.q: A trauma patient has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. What is this called and what does it suggest?
choices: Cushing's triad, suggesting rising intracranial pressure
Beck's triad, suggesting cardiac tamponade
Kussmaul's sign, suggesting constrictive pericarditis
Levine's sign, suggesting myocardial ischemia
checks.why: Beck's triad describes tamponade: blood in the pericardial sac prevents filling, so pressure falls while venous pressure rises and the heart sounds become distant. Cushing's triad is hypertension with bradycardia, a different pattern entirely.

checks.q: A patient's calf hurts when you dorsiflex the foot. How should you weight that finding?
choices: It confirms deep vein thrombosis
It excludes deep vein thrombosis if absent
It is Homans' sign, which is neither sensitive nor specific and should not drive decisions
It indicates arterial rather than venous disease
checks.why: Homans' sign performs poorly in both directions, so neither its presence nor its absence changes the probability much. Imaging and validated scoring tools are what settle the question.

checks.q: Which two eponyms both point to basilar skull fracture?
choices: Murphy's sign and Rovsing's sign
Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs
Battle's sign and raccoon eyes
Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs
checks.why: Bruising behind the ear over the mastoid and bruising around both orbits without direct eye trauma both indicate blood tracking from a basilar skull fracture. Chvostek's and Trousseau's indicate low calcium, and Brudzinski's and Kernig's indicate meningeal irritation.

lessons.title: Line by line: an EMS run sheet and an ED note
lessons.body:
## The run sheet, decoded

Here is a realistic prehospital narrative. Read it once, then read the decoding beneath it.

`Disp 1412 for 67M SOB. Arr 1419. Pt found seated tripod on edge of bed, A&Ox4, c/o SOB x2d, worse today. Hx COPD, CHF, HTN, DM2. NKDA. LS exp wheezes bilat, dim bases. Accessory muscle use, unable to speak full sentences. VS 1421: BP 156/92, HR 112 irr, RR 28, SpO2 88% RA, T 37.2 (oral), CBG 168, GCS 15. Tx: albuterol 2.5 mg / ipratropium 0.5 mg neb, semi-Fowler's, O2 titrated to SpO2 94%. Recheck 1432: RR 22, SpO2 94%, LS improved. Txp P2 to RMC. Rpt to RN, bed 9. Arr ED 1447.`

| Fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Disp 1412`, `Arr 1419` | Dispatched at 2:12 p.m., on scene at 2:19 p.m. |
| `67M SOB` | Sixty-seven-year-old male, shortness of breath |
| `tripod` | Sitting forward on braced arms, a work-of-breathing sign |
| `A&Ox4` | Alert and oriented to person, place, time and event |
| `c/o SOB x2d` | Complains of shortness of breath for two days |
| `Hx COPD, CHF, HTN, DM2` | History of chronic lung disease, heart failure, hypertension, type 2 diabetes |
| `NKDA` | No known drug allergies |
| `LS exp wheezes bilat, dim bases` | Lung sounds: expiratory wheezes on both sides, diminished at the bases |
| `SpO2 88% RA` | Oxygen saturation `88%` on room air |
| `CBG 168` | Capillary blood glucose `168 mg/dL` |
| `neb` | Nebulized, given as a mist |
| `Txp P2 to RMC` | Transported as priority 2 to the receiving hospital |
| `Rpt to RN` | Report given to the receiving nurse |

> **Key:** Every time stamp in that narrative is doing work. The gap between `1421` and `1432` is what proves the treatment helped, and without both sets the improvement is an opinion.

## The structures behind the narrative

Most EMS narratives follow one of two formats.

**`CHART`** — Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx (treatment), Transport.

**`SOAP`** — Subjective (what the patient says), Objective (what you measured), Assessment (what you think), Plan (what you did and will do).

Handoffs use a third structure, **`SBAR`**: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It exists because the recommendation is the part people forget to say out loud.

## The ED note, decoded

An emergency physician's note runs in a fixed order too.

1. **Chief complaint** — one phrase, usually the patient's words
2. **`HPI`**, history of present illness — the story, with onset, quality, timing and modifiers
3. **`ROS`**, review of systems — a checklist of symptoms by body system
4. **`PMH`, `PSH`, `FHx`, `SHx`** — past medical, past surgical, family and social history
5. **Allergies and medications**
6. **Physical exam** — by system
7. **`MDM`**, medical decision making — the reasoning, the differential, what was ruled in and out
8. **Disposition** — admit, discharge, transfer, observation

A line from the same patient's chart might read:

`67 yo M w/ hx COPD, CHF p/w 2d prog dyspnea, BIBA. VS on arrival T 37.2 P 112 R 28 BP 156/92 SpO2 88% RA. Exam: mod resp distress, diffuse exp wheeze, no JVD, 1+ BLE edema. CXR: mild cardiomegaly, no acute infiltrate. MDM: COPD exacerbation vs acute CHF; BNP pending. Plan: duonebs, steroids, admit tele.`

`p/w` is presents with, `prog` is progressive, `BIBA` is brought in by ambulance, `JVD` is jugular venous distension, `BLE` is bilateral lower extremity, `CXR` is chest radiograph, and `tele` is a telemetry bed with continuous cardiac monitoring.

> **Trap:** `w/` means with and `w/o` means without, and they are a single character apart in handwriting. In a line like `CP w/o radiation`, that character is the difference between a reassuring and an alarming chest pain description.

> **On shift:** Read the `MDM` section when you want to know what the physician is actually worried about. The exam and the orders tell you what was done; the `MDM` tells you why, and it is where the differential lives.
keyPoints: Time stamps are load-bearing: paired vitals before and after treatment are what prove an intervention worked.
EMS narratives follow CHART or SOAP; handoffs follow SBAR, where the recommendation is the commonly skipped part.
An ED note runs chief complaint, HPI, ROS, histories, allergies and meds, exam, MDM, and disposition.
The MDM section holds the differential and the reasoning, which is where the physician's actual concern lives.
w/ and w/o differ by one character and can invert the meaning of an entire finding.

checks.q: A run sheet reads: VS 1421 SpO2 88% RA, recheck 1432 SpO2 94% on neb. Why do both entries matter?
choices: Only the later value matters, since it reflects the current state
The paired timed values document that the treatment produced the improvement
The earlier value should be deleted once the patient improves
Two values are required only for unstable patients
checks.why: A before-and-after pair with time stamps is what converts an impression into evidence that the nebulizer worked. Deleting or omitting the first value destroys the trend the receiving team needs.

checks.q: Which section of an ED note tells you what the physician is actually worried about?
choices: Review of systems
Physical exam
Medical decision making
Chief complaint
checks.why: The MDM records the differential, the reasoning, and what was ruled in or out. The chief complaint and exam describe findings, and the review of systems is a symptom checklist.

checks.q: What does SBAR add that CHART and SOAP do not emphasize?
choices: A record of vital signs
An explicit recommendation at the end
The patient's allergy list
A time-stamped treatment log
checks.why: SBAR ends with the recommendation, the specific ask, which is the part most often left unsaid in a verbal handoff. Vitals, allergies and treatments appear in all of these formats.

lessons.title: Slang, shorthand and what people really mean
lessons.body:
## Three categories, not one

Informal language in a department falls into three groups, and they are not equivalent.

1. **Operational shorthand** — real, useful, and safe to use out loud
2. **Descriptive slang** — informal but not disrespectful, and still wrong in a chart
3. **Derogatory slang** — never acceptable, in a chart or out of it

> **Key:** The working test is simple. Would you say this sentence with the patient's family standing behind you? If not, it does not belong anywhere, including in the break room.

## Operational shorthand

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Code, coding | A cardiac arrest, or the arrest response itself |
| Code 3 | Lights and siren response |
| Trauma activation, level 1 | The whole trauma team is summoned before arrival |
| Boarder | An admitted patient still occupying an emergency department bed |
| Wall time, drop time | How long crews wait to transfer a patient at the hospital |
| Bounce back | A patient who returns shortly after discharge |
| Tubed | Intubated |
| Bagging | Ventilating with a bag-valve mask |
| Lines and tubes | Vascular access and any drainage or airway tubes in place |
| Drips | Continuous intravenous infusions |
| `LWBS` | Left without being seen |
| `AMA` | Left against medical advice |
| `MCI` | Mass casualty incident |
| Field termination | Resuscitation stopped on scene rather than transporting |

## Real clinical terms that sound like slang

Some words sound informal and are genuinely correct.

- **Obtunded** — a real level of consciousness: blunted, slow to respond, arousable with difficulty
- **Sundowning** — a real, described phenomenon of increased confusion in the late afternoon and evening, common in dementia
- **Rule out**, `r/o` — a legitimate diagnostic statement meaning this is being actively excluded
- **Guarding** and **rebound** — precise abdominal examination findings
- **Dry** and **wet** — accepted shorthand for volume depleted and volume overloaded

## Slang that must stay out of the chart

Terms like train wreck, frequent flyer, circling the drain and various acronyms invented to insult patients share three problems. They are inaccurate, because they substitute a label for a finding. They are discoverable, because charts are read by patients, lawyers and licensing boards. And they change your thinking, because a patient labelled a frequent flyer gets a less careful assessment the next time, and the next time is when the diagnosis is real.

> **Trap:** Documenting a patient as drunk is both slang and a diagnosis you have not made. The defensible chart entry describes what you observed, such as odor of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait, and glucose `96 mg/dL`, and lets someone else name the cause.

## Talking over a radio

Spoken shorthand fails differently than written shorthand, because the listener cannot ask the page to repeat itself.

- **`Hyper-` and `hypo-` sound nearly identical** over a radio. Say high blood sugar or low blood sugar.
- **Fifteen and fifty are routinely confused.** Say one-five or five-zero.
- **Read back every number** you are given: dose, rate, time, room.
- **Say the drug name in full.** No `MS`, no `MSO4`, no `MgSO4`.

> **On shift:** The single most valuable verbal habit is the read-back. Repeat any order or number aloud to the person who gave it, and wait for them to confirm. It takes three seconds and catches the entire class of errors that come from mishearing rather than misjudging.
keyPoints: Informal language splits into operational shorthand, descriptive slang, and derogatory slang; only the first is safe to use out loud.
The test is whether you would say it with the patient's family behind you.
Obtunded, sundowning, guarding, rebound and rule out sound informal but are real clinical terms.
Derogatory labels are inaccurate, discoverable in the record, and bias the next assessment of that patient.
Over a radio, say high or low rather than hyper or hypo, say one-five rather than fifteen, and read every number back.

checks.q: A patient arrives with alcohol on their breath and slurred speech. What is the defensible way to chart it?
choices: Patient is drunk
Odor of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait, glucose 96 mg/dL
Frequent flyer, intoxicated as usual
Patient appears to be under the influence, no further assessment needed
checks.why: Charting observations rather than a conclusion keeps the record accurate and keeps other causes of altered speech open, which is exactly why the glucose is documented. Labels close down thinking and are discoverable in the record.

checks.q: Which of these is a real clinical term rather than slang?
choices: Obtunded
Train wreck
Circling the drain
Frequent flyer
checks.why: Obtunded describes a specific level of consciousness: blunted responsiveness, arousable with difficulty. The other three are labels that substitute judgment for findings and bias future assessments.

checks.q: You receive a radio order for a dose. What is the single most valuable habit?
choices: Write it down and confirm later with the chart
Read the number back aloud and wait for confirmation
Repeat the order to your partner instead
Ask for the order to be sent in writing after the call
checks.why: Read-back to the person who gave the order catches mishearing at the moment it happens, which is the entire class of error that later written confirmation cannot prevent. It takes about three seconds.

lessons.title: Word parts by organ system: the review pass
lessons.body:
## Re-filing what you already know

You have learned the parts in the order the language builds them: roots, then prefixes, then suffixes. That order teaches decoding. It is the wrong order for recall on a shift, because a shift asks questions by body system.

This lesson re-files the same parts by system. Nothing here is new; the point is the second index.

## Cardiovascular

`cardi/o` heart, `angi/o` and `vas/o` vessel, `arteri/o` artery, `phleb/o` and `ven/o` vein, `hem/o` and `hemat/o` blood, `thromb/o` clot, `ather/o` fatty plaque, `erythr/o` red, `leuk/o` white.

Assembled: `endocarditis`, `cardiomyopathy`, `atherosclerosis`, `thrombophlebitis`, `angioplasty`, `hematoma`, `leukocytosis`.

## Respiratory

`pneum/o` and `pneumon/o` lung or air, `pulmon/o` lung, `rhin/o` nose, `laryng/o` voice box, `trache/o` windpipe, `bronch/o` airway branches, `pleur/o` lung lining, `thorac/o` chest, `spir/o` breathing, `-pnea` breathing, `-ectasis` expansion or dilation.

Assembled: `pneumothorax`, `bronchospasm`, `atelectasis`, `pleuritis`, `apnea`, `dyspnea`, `spirometry`, `tracheostomy`.

## Neurologic

`neur/o` nerve, `cephal/o` head, `encephal/o` brain, `cerebr/o` cerebrum, `mening/o` the coverings, `myel/o` cord or marrow, `-plegia` paralysis, `-paresis` weakness, `-phasia` speech, `-esthesia` sensation.

Assembled: `meningitis`, `encephalopathy`, `hemiparesis`, `aphasia`, `paresthesia`, `quadriplegia`, `neuropathy`.

## Gastrointestinal

`gastr/o` stomach, `enter/o` small intestine, `col/o` large intestine, `hepat/o` liver, `chol/e` bile, `cholecyst/o` gallbladder, `pancreat/o` pancreas, `proct/o` rectum and anus, `-emesis` vomiting, `-phagia` swallowing.

Assembled: `gastroenteritis`, `cholecystitis`, `cholelithiasis`, `hepatomegaly`, `hematemesis`, `dysphagia`, `colostomy`.

## Genitourinary

`nephr/o` and `ren/o` kidney, `pyel/o` renal pelvis, `cyst/o` bladder, `ur/o` and `urin/o` urine, `-uria` urine condition, `orchi/o` testis, `hyster/o` uterus, `salping/o` tube, `prostat/o` prostate.

Assembled: `pyelonephritis`, `nephrolithiasis`, `cystitis`, `hematuria`, `oliguria`, `polyuria`, `hysterectomy`.

## Musculoskeletal

`oste/o` bone, `arthr/o` joint, `my/o` muscle, `chondr/o` cartilage, `cost/o` rib, `crani/o` skull, `spondyl/o` and `vertebr/o` vertebra, `ten/o` tendon, `-algia` pain, `-desis` fusion, `-malacia` softening.

Assembled: `osteomyelitis`, `arthroscopy`, `myalgia`, `costochondritis`, `arthrodesis`, `tendinitis`.

## Skin and senses

`derm/o` and `dermat/o` skin, `cutane/o` skin, `onych/o` nail, `melan/o` black, `cyan/o` blue, `xer/o` dry, `ot/o` ear, `ophthalm/o` and `ocul/o` eye, `blephar/o` eyelid, `kerat/o` cornea.

Assembled: `dermatitis`, `subcutaneous`, `melanoma`, `cyanosis`, `otitis media`, `blepharoptosis`.

## Endocrine and metabolic

`glyc/o` and `gluc/o` sugar, `thyr/o` thyroid, `aden/o` gland, `natr/o` sodium, `kal/i` potassium, `calc/i` calcium, `-emia` blood condition.

Assembled: `hyperglycemia`, `hypoglycemia`, `hyperthyroidism`, `hyponatremia`, `hyperkalemia`, `adenopathy`.

> **Key:** The same suffix behaves identically in every system. `-itis` is inflammation whether it lands on `gastr`, `arthr`, `mening` or `derm`. You are not learning eight vocabularies; you are learning one, applied eight times.

## The five-minute self-test

Cover the lists and produce, from memory, one word per system that uses `-itis`, one that uses `-ectomy`, and one that uses `hyper-` or `hypo-`. If you can generate twenty-one words that way, the parts are filed correctly.

> **On the exam:** Questions are written by system, not by word part. A cardiac stem needs `cardi/o`, `angi/o`, `thromb/o` and `-emia` retrieved together in seconds. That is a different skill from decoding, and this is the lesson that builds it.
keyPoints: The same parts need a second index, filed by body system, because shifts ask questions by system.
Cardiovascular: cardi/o, angi/o, vas/o, arteri/o, phleb/o, thromb/o, ather/o, hem/o.
Respiratory: pneum/o, pulmon/o, bronch/o, pleur/o, thorac/o, spir/o, -pnea, -ectasis.
Genitourinary: nephr/o, ren/o, pyel/o, cyst/o, ur/o, -uria; musculoskeletal: oste/o, arthr/o, my/o, chondr/o, spondyl/o.
A suffix behaves identically in every system, so this is one vocabulary applied eight times, not eight vocabularies.

checks.q: Which root set belongs to the genitourinary system?
choices: cardi/o, angi/o, thromb/o
pneum/o, bronch/o, pleur/o
nephr/o, pyel/o, cyst/o
oste/o, arthr/o, chondr/o
checks.why: Kidney, renal pelvis and bladder are the genitourinary set. The others are cardiovascular, respiratory and musculoskeletal respectively.

checks.q: Decode pyelonephritis.
choices: Inflammation of the bladder
Inflammation of the renal pelvis and kidney
Stones in the renal pelvis
Surgical removal of the kidney
checks.why: Pyel/o is renal pelvis, nephr/o is kidney, and -itis is inflammation, so the infection has reached the kidney itself. Bladder inflammation is cystitis, stones are nephrolithiasis, and removal is nephrectomy.

checks.q: Why does filing word parts by body system help on an exam?
choices: Exams test spelling rather than meaning
Questions are written by system, so the relevant parts must be retrieved together in seconds
System filing replaces the need to decode
Each system uses a unique set of suffixes
checks.why: A cardiac vignette requires cardi/o, angi/o, thromb/o and -emia retrieved as a group, which is retrieval rather than decoding. Suffixes are shared across systems, and decoding remains essential for unfamiliar words.

cards.front: Which roots mean red, white, black and blue?
cards.back: Erythr/o red (erythrocyte), leuk/o white (leukocyte), melan/o black (melanoma), cyan/o blue (cyanosis).

cards.front: What is the difference between -penia and -osis?
cards.back: -penia is a deficiency and -osis is an abnormal condition, usually an excess. Leukopenia is too few white cells; leukocytosis is too many.

cards.front: Decode thrombocytopenia.
cards.back: Thromb/o clot, cyt/o cell, -penia deficiency: too few clotting cells, meaning low platelets. The opposite is thrombocytosis.

cards.front: What do -stenosis and -ectasis mean?
cards.back: -stenosis is narrowing, as in aortic stenosis. -ectasis is dilation or expansion, as in bronchiectasis or atelectasis.

cards.front: What do -rrhaphy, -desis and -tripsy mean?
cards.back: -rrhaphy is surgical suturing (herniorrhaphy), -desis is surgical fusion (arthrodesis), and -tripsy is crushing (lithotripsy).

cards.front: What do the prefixes pan-, neo-, mal- and iso- mean?
cards.back: Pan- is all (pancytopenia), neo- is new (neoplasm), mal- is bad or poor (malabsorption), iso- is equal or same (isotonic).

cards.front: What is the difference between ileum and ilium?
cards.back: Ileum is the last segment of small intestine; ilium is the flaring hip bone. Identical pronunciation, unrelated structures. An ileostomy opens bowel; the iliac crest is bone.

cards.front: What do -ptosis, -malacia and -trophy mean?
cards.back: -ptosis is drooping or falling (blepharoptosis), -malacia is softening (osteomalacia), -trophy is development or nourishment (hypertrophy, atrophy).

cards.front: What does hemolyzed mean on a specimen, and which value does it distort?
cards.back: Red cells broke during collection or transport. It falsely raises potassium, because potassium is mostly intracellular, so the specimen must be redrawn.

cards.front: What does a left shift on a differential mean?
cards.back: An increase in immature neutrophils, called bands. The marrow is releasing cells early, which suggests active infection.

cards.front: What is measured in a basic metabolic panel?
cards.back: Sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate (often labelled CO2), blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose and calcium. A comprehensive panel adds liver values.

cards.front: How do you name a high or low electrolyte in one word?
cards.back: Hyper- or hypo- plus the substance root plus -emia. Hyperkalemia is high potassium (kal/i), hyponatremia is low sodium (natr/o), hypercalcemia is high calcium.

cards.front: What question does each of troponin, BNP, D-dimer and lactate answer?
cards.back: Troponin: has heart muscle been damaged. BNP: is the heart stretched, as in heart failure. D-dimer: is there clot breakdown. Lactate: is tissue running without enough oxygen.

cards.front: What are the four sections of a radiology report, in order?
cards.back: Technique (what was done), comparison (the prior study), findings (everything observed, including normal), and impression (the conclusion, numbered by importance).

cards.front: What do radiopaque and radiolucent mean?
cards.back: Radiopaque blocks x-rays and appears white: bone, metal, contrast. Radiolucent passes x-rays and appears dark: air, fat. An opacity is whiter than expected; a lucency is darker.

cards.front: What do the report phrases no acute cardiopulmonary process and clinical correlation recommended actually mean?
cards.back: The first means nothing new and urgent was seen, not that the chest is normal. The second means imaging alone cannot settle it and the answer depends on the patient.

cards.front: What are the six parts of a complete medication order?
cards.back: Drug name, strength and dose form, route, frequency, duration or quantity, and indication. A missing part is a query to the prescriber, never an assumption.

cards.front: What do qhs, ac and pc mean?
cards.back: qhs is at bedtime (hora somni), ac is before meals (ante cibum), pc is after meals (post cibum).

cards.front: What is the practical difference between QID and q6h?
cards.back: Both total four doses. QID means four doses during waking hours; q6h means every six hours around the clock, including overnight, which keeps drug levels steadier.

cards.front: What do ER, XR, SR, CR, LA and DR mean on a tablet, and why does it matter?
cards.back: All mark a slow- or delayed-release formulation. They must not be crushed or split, because doing so releases the full dose at once.

cards.front: What do NS, D5W, LR and KVO mean on a fluid order?
cards.back: NS is normal saline, D5W is 5% dextrose in water, LR is lactated Ringer's, and KVO or TKO means run the line just fast enough to keep the vein open.

cards.front: What is a drop factor and what are the common values?
cards.back: The number of drops per milliliter delivered by a given IV tubing set, printed on the package. Commonly 10, 15 or 60 gtts/mL. Drip rates are written in gtts/min.

cards.front: Decode: Ondansetron 4 mg SL q8h PRN nausea, disp #20.
cards.back: Four milligrams dissolved under the tongue, every eight hours, only as needed for nausea, with twenty doses dispensed.

cards.front: Why is HS discouraged on medication orders?
cards.back: It means both at bedtime and half strength, two incompatible instructions. Write the words out. It sits on most institutional avoid lists for that reason.

cards.front: Distinguish tracheotomy, tracheostomy and tracheectomy.
cards.back: Tracheotomy cuts into the trachea as an act. Tracheostomy creates a lasting opening kept open. Tracheectomy removes the trachea itself.

cards.front: Distinguish thoracentesis, thoracostomy and thoracotomy.
cards.back: Thoracentesis is needle drainage of pleural fluid. Thoracostomy places a chest tube that stays. Thoracotomy is surgical opening of the chest.

cards.front: What is the difference between a craniotomy and a craniectomy?
cards.back: A craniotomy opens the skull and replaces the bone flap. A craniectomy leaves the flap off to allow for brain swelling, so that side of the head is unprotected.

cards.front: What do the approach words open, laparoscopic, percutaneous and endoscopic mean?
cards.back: Open is a full incision, laparoscopic is through small abdominal ports with a camera, percutaneous is through the skin with a needle or catheter, endoscopic is through a natural opening.

cards.front: Expand ORIF, CABG, PCI, THA and TKA.
cards.back: Open reduction internal fixation, coronary artery bypass graft (spoken as cabbage), percutaneous coronary intervention, total hip arthroplasty, total knee arthroplasty.

cards.front: What are a fasciotomy and an escharotomy, and why are they done?
cards.back: A fasciotomy cuts fascia to relieve compartment pressure. An escharotomy cuts through rigid burned skin to relieve constriction. Both restore circulation or ventilation.

cards.front: What does a lap chole mean, and what does POD 2 mean?
cards.back: A laparoscopic cholecystectomy: the gallbladder removed through small ports. POD 2 is postoperative day two.

cards.front: What is a surgical time-out?
cards.back: The mandatory pause before incision in which the whole team confirms patient identity, procedure and site out loud. It exists to prevent wrong-site and wrong-patient surgery.

cards.front: What is Murphy's sign and what does it suggest?
cards.back: Press under the right costal margin while the patient inhales; they stop the breath from pain. It suggests acute cholecystitis.

cards.front: What are Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs, and what is the timing catch?
cards.back: Cullen's is bruising around the umbilicus and Grey Turner's is bruising in the flanks, both from intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding. Both take 24–48 hours to appear.

cards.front: Which two findings point to basilar skull fracture?
cards.back: Battle's sign, bruising over the mastoid behind the ear, and raccoon eyes, bruising around both orbits without direct eye trauma.

cards.front: What is Beck's triad and what does it mean?
cards.back: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. It indicates cardiac tamponade: blood in the pericardial sac preventing the heart from filling.

cards.front: What are Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs?
cards.back: Both indicate low calcium. Chvostek's: tapping the facial nerve makes the face twitch. Trousseau's: a blood pressure cuff inflated for 3 minutes causes carpal spasm, and it is the more reliable.

cards.front: What are Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs?
cards.back: Both suggest meningeal irritation. Brudzinski's: flexing the neck makes the hips and knees flex. Kernig's: with the hip flexed, straightening the knee causes pain.

cards.front: Why should Homans' sign not drive decisions?
cards.back: Calf pain on dorsiflexion is neither sensitive nor specific for deep vein thrombosis, so a negative rules nothing out and a positive proves nothing. Imaging and validated scores settle it.

cards.front: Which two unrelated findings are both named after Kussmaul?
cards.back: Kussmaul respirations, deep fast sighing breaths from metabolic acidosis, and Kussmaul's sign, neck veins rising on inspiration in tamponade or constrictive pericarditis.

cards.front: What do CHART and SOAP stand for in an EMS narrative?
cards.back: CHART is Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx (treatment), Transport. SOAP is Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

cards.front: What does SBAR stand for and what does it add?
cards.back: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It adds the explicit ask at the end, which is the part most often left unsaid in a verbal handoff.

cards.front: Decode: Pt found seated tripod, A&Ox4, c/o SOB x2d, LS exp wheezes bilat, SpO2 88% RA.
cards.back: Found sitting forward on braced arms, alert and oriented to person, place, time and event, complaining of shortness of breath for two days, expiratory wheezes in both lungs, oxygen saturation 88% on room air.

cards.front: Name the sections of an ED note in order.
cards.back: Chief complaint, history of present illness, review of systems, past medical and surgical and family and social history, allergies and medications, physical exam, medical decision making, disposition.

cards.front: Which section of an ED note holds the differential, and why read it?
cards.back: Medical decision making. The exam and orders show what was done; the MDM shows why, including what the physician is worried about and what was ruled in or out.

cards.front: Decode: p/w 2d prog dyspnea, BIBA, no JVD, 1+ BLE edema, CXR mild cardiomegaly, admit tele.
cards.back: Presents with two days of progressive shortness of breath, brought in by ambulance, no jugular venous distension, mild swelling of both legs, chest radiograph shows a slightly enlarged heart, admitted to a monitored bed.

cards.front: Why are w/ and w/o dangerous in handwriting?
cards.back: They differ by a single character and invert the meaning. In a line like chest pain w/o radiation, that character separates a reassuring description from an alarming one.

cards.front: What are the three categories of informal language in a department?
cards.back: Operational shorthand, which is safe out loud; descriptive slang, informal but still wrong in a chart; and derogatory slang, never acceptable anywhere.

cards.front: What is the working test for whether a phrase is acceptable?
cards.back: Would you say it with the patient's family standing behind you? If not, it does not belong in the chart, on the radio, or in the break room.

cards.front: Name four terms that sound like slang but are real clinical language.
cards.back: Obtunded (blunted responsiveness, arousable with difficulty), sundowning (evening confusion in dementia), guarding and rebound (abdominal exam findings), and rule out.

cards.front: Give three reasons derogatory patient labels are harmful.
cards.back: They substitute a label for a finding, so they are inaccurate; charts are discoverable by patients, lawyers and boards; and they bias the next assessment, which is when the diagnosis turns out to be real.

cards.front: How should intoxication be charted?
cards.back: By observation, not conclusion: odor of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait, and the glucose value. Naming the cause is a diagnosis you have not made.

cards.front: Name three radio-communication habits that prevent mishearing.
cards.back: Say high or low blood sugar instead of hyper- or hypo-; say one-five and five-zero instead of fifteen and fifty; read every number back and wait for confirmation.

cards.front: What does LWBS mean, and how is it different from AMA?
cards.back: Left without being seen means the patient departed before evaluation. Against medical advice means they were evaluated and chose to leave despite a recommendation to stay.

cards.front: List the core cardiovascular roots.
cards.back: Cardi/o heart, angi/o and vas/o vessel, arteri/o artery, phleb/o and ven/o vein, hem/o and hemat/o blood, thromb/o clot, ather/o fatty plaque.

cards.front: List the core respiratory roots and suffixes.
cards.back: Pneum/o and pneumon/o lung or air, pulmon/o lung, rhin/o nose, laryng/o voice box, trache/o windpipe, bronch/o airway branches, pleur/o lining, thorac/o chest, spir/o breathing, -pnea breathing.

cards.front: List the core neurologic roots and suffixes.
cards.back: Neur/o nerve, cephal/o head, encephal/o brain, cerebr/o cerebrum, mening/o coverings, myel/o cord or marrow, with -plegia paralysis, -paresis weakness, -phasia speech, -esthesia sensation.

cards.front: List the core genitourinary roots.
cards.back: Nephr/o and ren/o kidney, pyel/o renal pelvis, cyst/o bladder, ur/o and urin/o urine, orchi/o testis, hyster/o uterus, salping/o tube, prostat/o prostate.

cards.front: Decode pyelonephritis and contrast it with cystitis.
cards.back: Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the renal pelvis and kidney, meaning infection has reached the kidney. Cystitis is bladder inflammation, a lower and less dangerous infection.

cards.front: Why does filing word parts by body system matter for exams?
cards.back: Questions are written by system, so a cardiac stem requires cardi/o, angi/o, thromb/o and -emia retrieved together in seconds. That is retrieval, a different skill from decoding.

quiz.q: A chart lists leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. What do those two terms describe?
choices: Too few white cells and too few platelets
Too many white cells and too many platelets
Too few white cells and too many platelets
Breakdown of white cells and platelets
quiz.why: -penia is deficiency in both terms. Excess would be leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, and breakdown would be -lysis. Reading the suffix first settles it immediately.

quiz.q: A radiology report mentions bronchiectasis in one patient and aortic stenosis in another. What is the structural difference being described?
choices: Both describe narrowing, in different vessels
Both describe inflammation
The first is abnormal dilation and the second is narrowing
The first is narrowing and the second is dilation
quiz.why: -ectasis is dilation or expansion, so bronchiectasis is permanently widened airways. -stenosis is narrowing, so aortic stenosis is a tightened valve. They are opposites and are frequently confused in reading.

quiz.q: A surgical note describes a herniorrhaphy and an arthrodesis performed in the same admission. What was done in each?
choices: The hernia was removed and the joint was replaced
The hernia was punctured and the joint was examined with a camera
The hernia was crushed and the joint was cut into
The hernia was sewn closed and the joint was surgically fused
quiz.why: -rrhaphy is suturing and -desis is surgical fusion. Removal would be -ectomy, puncture would be -centesis, camera inspection would be -scopy, and crushing would be -tripsy.

quiz.q: A patient's chart reads pancytopenia. A student reads it as pancreatic inflammation. What went wrong?
choices: Nothing; the two terms are synonymous
Pan- means all and cyt/o means cell, so it is a deficiency of all blood cell lines; the pancreas root is pancreat/o
-penia means inflammation rather than deficiency
Pan- is a shortened form of pancreat/o
quiz.why: Pan- is a prefix meaning all, and it is not related to pancreat/o. Inflammation is -itis, and pancreatic inflammation would be pancreatitis, an entirely different word.

quiz.q: A potassium of 6.6 mEq/L is reported with the comment specimen hemolyzed. What is the correct next step?
choices: Treat the hyperkalemia immediately and ignore the comment
Report the value as normal
Recognize that hemolysis falsely elevates potassium and arrange a redraw while continuing to assess the patient
Discard the result and order no further potassium
quiz.why: Ruptured red cells release intracellular potassium into the sample, falsely raising the reported value, so the specimen must be redrawn. A sick patient is not ignored in the meantime, but acting on a hemolyzed value alone risks treating an artifact.

quiz.q: A differential shows an increase in bands. What does this indicate?
choices: A left shift, meaning immature neutrophils are being released early, which suggests infection
An allergic reaction, since bands are eosinophils
A bleeding disorder from low platelets
Dehydration causing falsely high counts
quiz.why: Bands are immature neutrophils, and their rise is called a left shift because of how the cells were traditionally arranged on a report. Eosinophils rise in allergy and parasitic disease, and platelets are a separate line.

quiz.q: A chest radiograph on a patient with pleuritic chest pain reads: no acute cardiopulmonary process. What does that permit?
choices: Confident exclusion of pulmonary embolism
A conclusion that the chest is entirely normal
A conclusion that all chronic findings have resolved
Only the conclusion that no new emergency finding was seen on this study
quiz.why: The phrase addresses acute findings on that modality only. Chronic abnormalities may persist, and pulmonary embolism frequently produces a normal chest radiograph, which is exactly why it is worked up with other tests.

quiz.q: Which laboratory value most directly answers the question, is heart muscle being damaged?
choices: BNP
Troponin
D-dimer
Lactate
quiz.why: Troponin is a protein released by injured cardiac muscle. BNP reflects cardiac stretch in heart failure, D-dimer reflects clot breakdown, and lactate reflects tissue running anaerobically.

quiz.q: An order reads: Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 7 days. How many capsules are dispensed, and when are they taken?
choices: 28 capsules, four times a day during waking hours
28 capsules, every six hours around the clock
21 capsules, three times a day
14 capsules, twice a day
quiz.why: QID is four times daily, so 4 times 7 is 28 capsules, clustered into waking hours. q6h would be the around-the-clock version, TID gives 21 and BID gives 14.

quiz.q: A patient with a feeding tube is prescribed a tablet marked ER. What is the concern?
choices: ER tablets are always liquid-filled and cannot be given by tube
ER means emergency-release and requires a physician to administer it
ER marks extended release, so crushing it to pass through the tube delivers the whole dose at once
ER means the tablet is enteric coated and should be dissolved in acid first
quiz.why: ER, XR, SR, CR, LA and DR all indicate slow or delayed release. Crushing defeats that design and releases the entire dose immediately, which can be dangerous. The prescriber must be asked for an alternative formulation.

quiz.q: An order reads: furosemide 40 mg PO HS. Why should this be clarified?
choices: The dose is too high for oral administration
HS can mean at bedtime or half strength
PO cannot be used with furosemide
The order is missing an indication, which is the only problem
quiz.why: HS carries two incompatible meanings and sits on most institutional avoid lists, so the frequency is genuinely ambiguous. A missing indication is also worth clarifying but is not the dangerous element here.

quiz.q: Which order line is complete?
choices: Ibuprofen 600 mg q6h PRN
Ibuprofen PO q6h PRN pain
Ibuprofen 600 mg PO PRN pain
Ibuprofen 600 mg PO q6h PRN pain, disp #30
quiz.why: A complete order carries drug, strength, route, frequency, quantity and indication. The first omits the route, the second omits the strength, and the third omits the frequency, so each requires a call back to the prescriber.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has a tube placed between the ribs to drain blood from the pleural space, and it is secured to stay. What is the procedure name?
choices: Thoracotomy
Thoracentesis
Thoracostomy
Pericardiocentesis
quiz.why: A tube creating a lasting opening is -ostomy. Thoracotomy is surgical opening of the chest, thoracentesis is temporary needle drainage, and pericardiocentesis drains the sac around the heart.

quiz.q: A patient returns from neurosurgery after a craniectomy. Which precaution follows directly from that word?
choices: The bone flap was left off, so no pressure may be applied to that side of the head
The skull was opened and closed, so normal positioning is fine
The brain was removed in part, so no positioning matters
The procedure was endoscopic, so there is no incision to protect
quiz.why: -ectomy means removal, so the bone flap is gone and the brain is unprotected on that side. A craniotomy, by contrast, replaces the flap. Many craniectomy patients wear a protective helmet until the flap is replaced.

quiz.q: A patient with a severely burned, circumferentially charred forearm has a weakening radial pulse. Which procedure name describes the likely intervention?
choices: Fasciotomy
Amputation
Arthrodesis
Escharotomy
quiz.why: Escharotomy cuts through the rigid burned skin, the eschar, to relieve the tourniquet effect and restore circulation. Fasciotomy releases deeper compartment pressure and is a different indication; arthrodesis fuses a joint.

quiz.q: A handoff says the patient had a lap chole two days ago. What does that mean?
choices: Laparoscopic colectomy, two days ago
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy, two days ago
Laparotomy for cholangitis, planned in two days
Laparoscopic colostomy, two days ago
quiz.why: Lap is laparoscopic and chole refers to the gallbladder, with the -ectomy implied. Colon procedures use col/o, and a colostomy creates an opening rather than removing an organ.

quiz.q: A trauma patient is hypotensive with distended neck veins and heart sounds that are difficult to hear. Which eponym describes this and what does it indicate?
choices: Beck's triad, indicating cardiac tamponade
Cushing's triad, indicating rising intracranial pressure
Kehr's sign, indicating splenic rupture
Grey Turner's sign, indicating retroperitoneal bleeding
quiz.why: Beck's triad is hypotension, jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds, the classic tamponade picture. Cushing's triad involves hypertension with bradycardia, Kehr's is referred shoulder pain, and Grey Turner's is flank bruising.

quiz.q: A patient struck in the left flank complains of left shoulder pain that worsens lying flat, with no shoulder injury. What is this and what does it suggest?
choices: Levine's sign, suggesting cardiac pain
Rovsing's sign, suggesting appendicitis
Kehr's sign, suggesting blood irritating the diaphragm from a splenic injury
Battle's sign, suggesting a skull fracture
quiz.why: Blood under the left diaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve, which refers pain to the left shoulder and worsens when lying flat. Levine's is a gesture over the sternum, Rovsing's is an abdominal maneuver, and Battle's is mastoid bruising.

quiz.q: A patient's hand goes into spasm while a blood pressure cuff is inflated for three minutes. What does this suggest?
choices: Deep vein thrombosis in the arm
Low calcium, as Trousseau's sign
Rising intracranial pressure
Compartment syndrome of the forearm
quiz.why: Trousseau's sign is carpal spasm induced by cuff inflation and indicates hypocalcemia; it is more reliable than Chvostek's facial tap. Cuff inflation does not test for thrombosis or intracranial pressure.

quiz.q: A blunt abdominal trauma patient has no periumbilical or flank bruising two hours after injury. What can you conclude?
choices: Intra-abdominal bleeding has been excluded
Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs are sensitive early findings, so bleeding is unlikely
The patient should be discharged
Nothing, because those signs take 24–48 hours to appear
quiz.why: Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs require time for blood to track to the skin and are absent early even with significant bleeding. Their absence at two hours is uninformative and must not be used to exclude injury.

quiz.q: A run sheet records SpO2 88% RA at 1421 and SpO2 94% on neb at 1432. Why is the earlier entry essential?
choices: It is required by law regardless of clinical value
It confirms the pulse oximeter was working
The paired timed values document that the nebulizer produced the improvement
It establishes the patient's baseline for future visits only
quiz.why: A single value shows where the patient is; two timed values show the direction and attribute the change to the treatment given between them. Deleting the earlier value destroys the evidence that anything worked.

quiz.q: You want to know what diagnosis the emergency physician was most concerned about. Which section do you read?
choices: Medical decision making
Review of systems
Physical exam
Chief complaint
quiz.why: The MDM records the differential and the reasoning, including what was ruled in and out. The chief complaint states the presenting problem, the exam records findings, and the review of systems is a symptom checklist.

quiz.q: Decode this fragment: 74F BIBA, p/w 3d prog SOB, hx CHF, 2+ BLE edema, no JVD, CXR cardiomegaly.
choices: 74-year-old female, walked in, three days of chest pain, no leg swelling
74-year-old male, brought by ambulance, three hours of shortness of breath, normal chest film
74-year-old female, brought by ambulance, three days of progressive chest pain, no edema

74-year-old female, brought in by ambulance, presenting with three days of progressive shortness of breath, history of heart failure, moderate swelling of both legs, no jugular venous distension, enlarged heart on chest radiograph
quiz.why: BIBA is brought in by ambulance, p/w is presents with, prog is progressive, SOB is shortness of breath, BLE is bilateral lower extremity, JVD is jugular venous distension, and CXR is chest radiograph. Each other option changes at least one element.

quiz.q: Which element does SBAR add that CHART and SOAP do not emphasize?
choices: A treatment log with times
An explicit recommendation, the specific ask
The allergy list
The patient's own words about the complaint
quiz.why: SBAR ends with the recommendation, which is the part that most commonly goes unsaid in verbal handoffs and the reason the format exists. Treatments, allergies and subjective statements appear in all three formats.

quiz.q: A patient smells of alcohol and has slurred speech after a fall. Which chart entry is defensible?
choices: Odor of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait, glucose 96 mg/dL, GCS 14
Patient is drunk and uncooperative
Frequent flyer, intoxicated again
Obviously under the influence; no further workup needed
quiz.why: Observations keep other causes of altered speech open, which is why the glucose and GCS are documented alongside them. Naming intoxication as the cause is a diagnosis you have not made, and labels are both inaccurate and discoverable.

quiz.q: Which term is a legitimate clinical descriptor rather than slang?
choices: Circling the drain
Train wreck
Obtunded
Status dramaticus
quiz.why: Obtunded names a specific level of consciousness: blunted, slow, arousable with difficulty. The others are labels that replace observation with judgment and carry no clinical information.

quiz.q: You are given a verbal medication order over a noisy radio. Which habit most reliably prevents a mishearing error?
choices: Writing it down for later verification against the chart
Reading the order and the numbers back aloud and waiting for confirmation
Asking a partner to listen simultaneously
Requesting written confirmation after the call
quiz.why: Read-back closes the loop at the moment of transmission, which is the only point at which a mishearing can be caught before it becomes an action. Later verification, a second listener and written confirmation all arrive after the dose could be given.

quiz.q: Why is saying hypoglycemia over a radio discouraged?
choices: It is too technical for dispatch to record
It is not a real diagnosis
It is on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list
Hyper- and hypo- sound nearly identical over a radio, and the two states call for opposite responses
quiz.why: Spoken over a poor connection, the prefixes are almost indistinguishable, and confusing them inverts the treatment. Saying low blood sugar or high blood sugar removes the ambiguity. Neither prefix is on the Do Not Use list.

quiz.q: A patient has a fever, flank pain and pyuria. Which term names infection that has reached the kidney itself?
choices: Cystitis
Nephrolithiasis
Pyelonephritis
Nephrectomy
quiz.why: Pyel/o is renal pelvis, nephr/o is kidney and -itis is inflammation, so the infection has ascended past the bladder. Cystitis is bladder infection, nephrolithiasis is kidney stones, and nephrectomy is surgical removal.

quiz.q: An NREMT stem describes a patient with clot in a leg vein and asks for the correct term. Which root set should you retrieve first?
choices: thromb/o and phleb/o, giving thrombophlebitis
arthr/o and oste/o, giving osteoarthritis
pyel/o and nephr/o, giving pyelonephritis
bronch/o and spir/o, giving bronchospasm
quiz.why: Thromb/o is clot and phleb/o is vein, so the combination with -itis names an inflamed vein containing a clot. The others belong to the musculoskeletal, genitourinary and respiratory systems and cannot describe a venous clot.

scenarios.title: Classroom: reading a discharge prescription set out loud
scenarios.intro: A 64-year-old is going home after a two-day admission for a chronic lung disease flare. You are handed the discharge medication list and asked to read it back to the patient in plain words, flagging anything that needs clarification before it leaves the department.

steps.prompt:
First line: `Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x 5 days, then stop.`

How do you read this to the patient?

choices.text: Forty milligrams by mouth once a day for five days, then stop completely
choices.feedback: Correct. Drug, strength, route, frequency, duration, all present. This line needs no clarification, and the explicit stop instruction is doing useful work.

choices.text: Forty milligrams by mouth four times a day for five days
choices.feedback: Wrong. Nothing in the line says four times a day. Daily is daily. Inventing a frequency is exactly the assumption error this module keeps returning to.

choices.text: Forty milligrams, route unspecified, once daily
choices.feedback: Over-cautious. PO is present and unambiguous: by mouth. Flagging a part that is actually there slows the process without adding safety.

choices.text: Read the line aloud verbatim, abbreviations included
choices.feedback: Not useful to the patient. The whole point of the read-back is converting shorthand into words the person taking the drug can act on.

steps.prompt:
Second line: `Albuterol MDI ii puffs q4h PRN SOB.`

What does it say?

choices.text: Two puffs from the inhaler, up to every four hours, only when short of breath
choices.feedback: Correct. The lowercase Roman numeral ii is two, MDI is a metered-dose inhaler, q4h is the minimum interval, and PRN means only when the symptom is present.

choices.text: Eleven puffs every four hours
choices.feedback: This is the classic Roman numeral misread. Lowercase ii is two. Reading it as eleven would be a more than fivefold overdose instruction.

choices.text: Two puffs every four hours around the clock, including overnight
choices.feedback: Close but wrong on one word. PRN means as needed, so the patient takes it only when short of breath. Around the clock would be ATC.

choices.text: Two puffs as needed, with no maximum frequency
choices.feedback: Incomplete. The q4h sets the minimum interval between doses, which is a real limit the patient needs to hear.

steps.prompt:
Third line: `Azithromycin 250 mg PO, i tab daily x 4 days.`

Fourth line: `Pantoprazole 40 mg PO qhs.`

What do these say, and how many azithromycin tablets are dispensed?

choices.text: Azithromycin one 250 mg tablet by mouth daily for four days, so four tablets; pantoprazole 40 mg by mouth at bedtime
choices.feedback: Correct on both. The lowercase i is one tablet, and qhs means at bedtime, from hora somni. Four days at one tablet daily is four tablets.
