choices.text: Azithromycin 250 mg four times a day for four days, so sixteen tablets
choices.feedback: Wrong. Daily is once a day. The i is the quantity per dose, not the frequency, and conflating the two multiplies the dose fourfold.

choices.text: Azithromycin four tablets; pantoprazole 40 mg half strength
choices.feedback: Half right. qhs is unambiguously at bedtime. HS is the abbreviation that can mean half strength, and that is precisely why qhs is written with the q.

choices.text: Azithromycin four tablets; pantoprazole 40 mg every hour
choices.feedback: No. There is no hourly frequency here. qhs is at bedtime; every hour would be q1h, which is not a realistic order for this drug.

steps.prompt:
Last line, handwritten on the printout: `Warfarin 5.0 mg PO daily, adjust per INR.`

What do you do?

choices.text: Flag it: the trailing zero makes 5.0 mg readable as 50 mg, and it must be rewritten as 5 mg
choices.feedback: Exactly. A trailing zero becomes a tenfold error the moment the decimal point smudges, faxes poorly or scans badly, and warfarin is a narrow-margin drug. This is a rewrite, not an interpretation.

choices.text: Read it as 5 mg and hand it over, since the intent is obvious
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Your reading is probably correct, and the patient, pharmacist and next clinician still receive a line that can be misread. Guessing right nine times does not offset the tenth.

choices.text: Flag that the indication is missing, which is the only problem with the line
choices.feedback: The indication is worth adding, but it is not the dangerous element. The trailing zero is the item that can produce a tenfold overdose of an anticoagulant.

choices.text: Flag that INR should be spelled out as international normalized ratio
choices.feedback: Unnecessary. INR is a standard, unambiguous abbreviation. Spending your one flag there means the trailing zero goes out the door.

scenarios.debrief:
Four lines, four different skills. The prednisone line was complete and needed nothing, which is worth practicing so that flagging stays meaningful. The albuterol line tested lowercase Roman numerals, where ii is two and misreading it as eleven is a documented error. The azithromycin line tested the difference between quantity per dose and frequency, where i tab daily is one tablet once, not four.

The warfarin line is the one to carry. Never write a trailing zero and always write a leading zero. Both rules exist because the decimal point is the least reliable mark on a page, and the drug in this case has a narrow margin between therapeutic and bleeding.

The habit underneath all four is the same: convert shorthand into plain words out loud, and treat any missing or ambiguous part as a question for the prescriber rather than a gap you fill from memory.

scenarios.title: ED: taking a handoff and turning it into a note
scenarios.intro: You are at the ambulance bay when a crew rolls in with a patient. You have about forty seconds of verbal report, and you will be expected to give the same information to the nurse taking the bed, then see it appear in the chart.

steps.prompt:
The medic says: `58F, BIBA from home. c/o CP x45min, substernal, radiating to L arm, 8/10, assoc N/V and diaphoresis. Hx HTN, DM2, hyperlipidemia. NKDA. s/p ASA 324 PO and NTG SL x1 PTA. VS: BP 148/88, HR 96, RR 20, SpO2 96% RA, CBG 184. 12-lead transmitted, no STEMI.`

What is the patient's story in plain words?

choices.text: A 58-year-old woman brought by ambulance from home with 45 minutes of central chest pain radiating to the left arm, rated 8 out of 10, with nausea, vomiting and sweating
choices.feedback: Correct. c/o is complains of, substernal is behind the breastbone, assoc N/V is associated nausea and vomiting, and diaphoresis is sweating. That combination is a classic cardiac presentation.

choices.text: A 58-year-old man with 45 minutes of chest pain and no associated symptoms
choices.feedback: Two errors. F is female, and assoc N/V and diaphoresis are exactly the associated symptoms that raise concern for a cardiac cause. Dropping them changes the clinical weight of the case.

choices.text: A 58-year-old woman with chest pain for 45 minutes and a history of a previous heart attack
choices.feedback: No previous heart attack was reported. The history given is hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol. Adding history nobody stated is as dangerous as dropping it.

choices.text: A 58-year-old woman with chest pain, currently pain free after nitroglycerin
choices.feedback: Not stated. She received nitroglycerin before arrival, but nobody said the pain resolved. Assuming a treatment worked without a repeat assessment is exactly what a second set of vitals exists to settle.

steps.prompt:
The medic said `s/p ASA 324 PO and NTG SL x1 PTA`.

What happened before she arrived?

choices.text: She received 324 mg of aspirin by mouth and one nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue before arrival
choices.feedback: Correct. s/p is status post, meaning after; ASA is aspirin; PO is by mouth; NTG is nitroglycerin; SL is sublingual; x1 is one dose; PTA is prior to arrival.

choices.text: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are planned but have not been given
choices.feedback: Backwards. s/p means status post, which is after the fact. PTA confirms it happened prior to arrival. Reading a completed treatment as a plan means the doses could be repeated.

choices.text: She received 324 mg of aspirin intravenously
choices.feedback: PO is by mouth, not intravenous. Aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain is given orally and chewed. Route errors are among the easiest and most consequential misreads.

choices.text: She received three nitroglycerin tablets under the tongue
choices.feedback: x1 is one dose. Three would be written x3. Nitroglycerin dosing in this setting is typically up to three doses five minutes apart, so the number is genuinely load-bearing.

steps.prompt:
You now give report to the nurse taking bed 6. She is in the middle of another task and has about twenty seconds.

Which structure do you use, and what must not be left out?

choices.text: SBAR, and the recommendation must not be left out: this needs a repeat 12-lead and a troponin now
choices.feedback: Correct. Situation, background, assessment and then the explicit ask. The recommendation is the element that routinely gets dropped, and in a possible cardiac case it is the one that starts the clock.

choices.text: Read the run sheet aloud from the top, in full
choices.feedback: Too slow and unfiltered. A twenty-second window forces prioritization, and the run sheet is written in chronological order rather than order of importance.

choices.text: Give the vital signs only and let her read the rest
choices.feedback: Insufficient. The vitals here are the least alarming part of the case. The story, the risk factors, the prehospital treatments and the ask are what change what happens next.

choices.text: Use SOAP, since it is the standard narrative format
choices.feedback: SOAP is a good documentation structure but it has no recommendation step, which is exactly what a verbal handoff needs. SBAR exists for this moment.

steps.prompt:
Later you read the physician's note. The medical decision making section says: `ACS vs GERD vs MSK. Initial trop neg, ECG nonischemic. Given risk factors and classic radiation, will serial trop and obs. Clinical correlation with repeat ECG in 2h.`

What is the physician saying?

choices.text: The heart has been ruled out and the cause is reflux
choices.feedback: The opposite. ACS is listed first, the plan is serial troponins and observation, and a repeat ECG is scheduled. A single negative troponin early does not exclude a heart attack.

choices.text: Acute coronary syndrome, reflux and a musculoskeletal cause are all still on the list; the first troponin and ECG are unremarkable, so she will be observed with repeat testing
choices.feedback: Correct reading. The MDM is where the differential lives, and this one keeps the cardiac diagnosis open explicitly because of her risk factors and the classic radiation pattern.

choices.text: The ECG was abnormal and she is going to the catheterization lab
choices.feedback: Nonischemic means the ECG did not show ischemic changes. Nothing here describes a catheterization plan, and the transmitted 12-lead in the field showed no STEMI.

choices.text: Nothing actionable; MDM sections are administrative
choices.feedback: Wrong, and this is the point of reading it. The MDM is the only section that states what the physician is worried about and what would change the plan.

scenarios.debrief:
The same patient appeared in three languages in twenty minutes: a spoken handoff dense with abbreviations, a verbal report you gave under time pressure, and a written note with its own structure.

Three specific things carried across all of them. s/p plus PTA means a treatment already happened, so reading it as a plan risks a repeated dose. x1 means one dose, and nitroglycerin dosing makes that number matter. And the MDM section is where the physician records the differential, which is why it is the section to read when you want to know what anyone is actually worried about.

The handoff structure is the practical takeaway. SOAP and CHART organize documentation; SBAR organizes speech, and it ends with a recommendation because that is the element people forget to say out loud. In this case the ask, a repeat 12-lead and a troponin now, was the sentence that mattered most.
